concepts.label: Historical linguistics
concepts.learning_takeaway: Track changes through competing variants rather than treating a language as fixed across generations.
concepts.card: Historical linguistics studies how languages change over time. Some variants remain stable alternatives, while others spread and replace older patterns. Comparing such changes can reveal shifts in pronunciation, grammar, or social influence, without assuming that every difference between today's speakers represents a change in progress.
concepts.original_description: study of language change over time

evidence.note: Checked variation-versus-change distinction; broad language-history wording does not treat every contemporary variant as a chronological stage.

relations.note: Change from above is one supported route through which language changes historically; it is an example within the field, not its complete definition.

imported_records.description: study of language change over time

concepts.label: Variationist sociolinguistics
concepts.learning_takeaway: Analyze how linguistic and social conditions alter the probability of variants in language as actually used.
concepts.card: Variationist sociolinguistics studies language as people use it, asking how social settings and linguistic environments influence variation. Instead of imagining one perfectly uniform speaker, it examines patterns across actual speech. A person may use the same variant at different rates when chatting casually and reading aloud.

evidence.note: Checked focus on usage, social/linguistic context, and casual-versus-reading example; no fixed speech stereotype is assigned to a social group.

evidence.locator: §10.7, Labov comparison of casual speech and reading
evidence.note: Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The variationist introduction and social-status example explicitly study context-dependent variant frequencies, including systematic style shifting.

relations.note: The variationist introduction and social-status example explicitly study context-dependent variant frequencies, including systematic style shifting.

concepts.label: Sociolinguistic interview
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare speech across tasks that elicit different levels of self-monitoring, or collect natural conversation.
concepts.card: A sociolinguistic interview gathers speech for studying variation. Tasks such as reading passages, pronouncing word pairs, and casual conversation can elicit different levels of self-monitoring. Researchers tailor the format to their question; an interview seeking natural conversation need not use every traditional task.

evidence.note: Checked traditional tasks and the source's tailoring caveat; not all sociolinguistic interviews are formal question lists or identical protocols.

evidence.locator: §10.7, Labov comparison of casual speech and reading
evidence.note: Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The methods chapter explicitly designs interview tasks to elicit varying self-monitoring and compare contextual styles.

relations.note: The methods chapter explicitly designs interview tasks to elicit varying self-monitoring and compare contextual styles.

concepts.label: Observer's paradox in sociolinguistics
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize that systematically recording everyday speech may change the very speech researchers want to observe.
concepts.card: The observer's paradox in sociolinguistics is that researchers want to study how people speak when they are not being observed, yet must observe them to collect evidence. A recording or unfamiliar interviewer can change self-monitoring, so natural rapport helps but cannot guarantee completely unmonitored speech.

evidence.note: Checked observation/self-monitoring tension and absence of a foolproof elicitation method; not equated with experimenter expectancy or socially desirable answers generally.

relations.note: The methods chapter explicitly identifies the observer's paradox as a central difficulty in obtaining vernacular speech through interviews.

concepts.label: Principle of accountability in sociolinguistics
concepts.learning_takeaway: Count every eligible variant to form a denominator instead of counting only the interesting pronunciation.
concepts.card: The sociolinguistic principle of accountability requires counting all occasions when a variant could occur, not only the instances that attract attention. Ten examples in one setting may represent a lower usage rate than eight in another. The relevant denominator makes comparisons across speaking contexts interpretable.

evidence.note: Checked eligible alternatives and count-versus-rate distinction in the source table; no rate inferred without the opportunity denominator.
Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The quantitative-analysis section explicitly names this denominator rule as a foundation of variationist sociolinguistic analysis.

relations.note: The quantitative-analysis section explicitly names this denominator rule as a foundation of variationist sociolinguistic analysis.

concepts.label: Sociolinguistic corpus
concepts.learning_takeaway: Combine recordings across a relevant speaker sample so community patterns can be distinguished from individual habits.
concepts.card: A sociolinguistic corpus brings together records of language use so patterns can be studied beyond one person's conversation. Collections may include interviews, letters, or other speech and writing. Which speakers and contexts are represented matters when interpreting a pattern as characteristic of a wider community.

evidence.note: Checked collection types and representative sampling concern; a corpus is not automatically representative or restricted to interviews.

relations.note: The source describes collections of interviews as sociolinguistic corpora while also allowing written and other recorded material.

concepts.label: Style shifting
concepts.learning_takeaway: Observe speakers changing variant frequencies with speaking context rather than assigning one fixed style to each class.
concepts.card: Style shifting is a change in how a speaker uses linguistic variants across situations. Labov's New York study compared casual speech with reading aloud and found systematic differences in variant frequencies. Such shifts show that describing someone's language with one unchanging social label misses variation within that person's usage.

evidence.locator: §10.7, Labov comparison of casual speech and reading
evidence.note: Checked contextual frequencies and named study; not claimed that every speaker changes in an identical direction or amount.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The methods and social-status chapters explicitly connect interview contexts and Labov's casual-speech/reading comparisons to style shifting.

relations.note: The methods and social-status chapters explicitly connect interview contexts and Labov's casual-speech/reading comparisons to style shifting.

concepts.label: Linguistic change from above
concepts.learning_takeaway: Trace consciously noticed adoption of a prestigious outside variant, illustrated by New York City's rhoticity shift.
concepts.card: A linguistic change from above spreads with social awareness, often through adoption of a prestigious variant from outside a community. Increasing rhoticity in New York English is a textbook example. Above refers to awareness of the change, rather than simply locating its speakers at the top of society.

evidence.note: Checked awareness-based definition and rhoticity example; the wording avoids confusing awareness with a universal top-down social-class origin.

relations.note: The source classifies this as a kind of language change; it is placed within historical linguistic inquiry without making prestige the explanation for every change.

concepts.label: Linguistic change from below
concepts.learning_takeaway: Trace language-system changes that spread below conscious social awareness, such as gradual vowel fronting.
concepts.card: A linguistic change from below develops largely outside speakers' conscious awareness. The textbook illustrates it with the goose vowel moving forward in Canadian English. Speakers can participate in a shifting pronunciation pattern without noticing it, unlike consciously adopting a prestigious form recognized as different.

evidence.note: Checked Canadian vowel example and conscious-awareness distinction; no claim that every unrecognized pronunciation difference is historical change.

relations.note: The source explicitly contrasts below-awareness system changes with socially noticed changes from above.

concepts.label: Atlas linguistique de la France
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how mapped transcriptions from many places make regional language variation inspectable.
concepts.card: The Atlas linguistique de la France turned regional speech observations into maps. Around the turn of the twentieth century, fieldwork gathered detailed transcriptions from hundreds of French locations. The atlas shows how systematically placing comparable forms on maps can make geographical variation visible rather than merely listing local words.

evidence.note: Checked survey scale, transcription and mapping; omitted the source's apparent fieldworker-name typo rather than reproducing it.

relations.note: The atlas is a named collection of geographically organized language observations, providing a historical comparison with modern sociolinguistic corpora.

concepts.label: Fangyan
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore how a Han-era collection of regional words preserves evidence used to infer earlier dialect groupings.
concepts.card: Fangyan is a Han-era collection of regional words associated with the scholar Yang Xiong. By recording different expressions and pronunciations across places, it preserved evidence about linguistic diversity. Later scholars used that material to infer earlier dialect groupings, showing how a vocabulary work can become historical evidence.

evidence.locator: §10.5, Dialectology: Then and now, Yang Xiong paragraph
evidence.note: Checked regional vocabulary, Yang Xiong attribution, and later scholarly use; no unverified precise date or exhaustive dialect classification is asserted.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The methods chapter describes later inferences about earlier dialect groups from Fangyan, linking the particular work to historical language study.

relations.note: The methods chapter describes later inferences about earlier dialect groups from Fangyan, linking the particular work to historical language study.

concepts.label: William Labov
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how occupation, education, and income were used to compare linguistic variant frequencies across social strata.
concepts.card: William Labov's study of New York speech compared linguistic variation with occupation, education, and income. It also examined differences between casual speech and reading. The case shows how social categories become research variables and why contextual variation must be considered alongside differences between groups.

evidence.note: Checked the three social measures and two contexts; correlations are not described as proof that class causes a pronunciation.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The textbook explicitly presents Labov's study as an example of quantitative sociolinguistic analysis of social status and speaking style.

relations.note: The textbook explicitly presents Labov's study as an example of quantitative sociolinguistic analysis of social status and speaking style.

concepts.label: Chantale Cenerini
concepts.learning_takeaway: Learn from her account of documenting community stories while respecting distinct local Michif and Métis language histories.
concepts.card: Chantale Cenerini describes documenting stories with Michif and Métis communities as work that can preserve language, family histories, and locally valued knowledge. Her account emphasizes learning each community's linguistic history first. A shared national identity does not mean every community uses the same language.

evidence.locator: §9.7, interview on local context and community stories
evidence.note: Checked first-person account and community-specific language histories; no universal claim about every Métis speaker or documentation project's outcome.

relations.note: Cenerini's interview directly describes her story-recording work and its language-documentation and family-legacy purposes.

concepts.label: Language documentation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Create records of language use and community knowledge that can serve both research and family legacies.
concepts.card: Language documentation creates records of language use and the knowledge expressed through it. Recording community stories can preserve family histories as well as linguistic forms. Such records may support future work, but making an archive is different from ensuring that people continue learning and using the language.

evidence.note: Checked story-recording and family-legacy functions; explicitly avoided treating documentation as sufficient evidence of revitalization.

relations.note: The Michif case distinguishes preserving records from choosing locally appropriate reclamation priorities; documentation and sustained use are connected but not equivalent.

concepts.label: Community-led language reclamation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Let communities' own language histories and goals guide locally tailored reclamation work rather than assuming one shared language.
concepts.card: Community-led language reclamation begins with a community's own history and goals. Cenerini's Michif case explains that Métis communities do not all share one language, so a uniform national approach can miss local identities. Learning what people speak and value shapes which reclamation work makes sense there.

evidence.note: Checked the approved local-history/goals condition and multilingual-community qualification; no generic replacement of the baseline revitalization identity.

relations.note: Cenerini's local-history emphasis can guide the purposes of documentation; the link preserves the governance distinction instead of renaming generic revitalization.

concepts.label: Peer learning
concepts.learning_takeaway: Develop understanding by explaining reasoning to other learners and considering their explanations.
concepts.card: Peer learning develops understanding through exchanges between learners. Explaining why an answer seems right and listening to another person's reasoning can expose gaps that solitary work misses. Peer Instruction provides one structured classroom example, but the broader activity is not limited to that particular voting-and-discussion sequence.
concepts.original_description: Developing understanding through collaboration and exchange among learners.

evidence.note: Checked reasoning exchange and specific protocol example; no guarantee that every peer discussion corrects errors or improves learning.

relations.note: The Peer Instruction paper explicitly describes learners explaining reasoning to each other within a collaborative classroom protocol.

imported_records.description: Developing understanding through collaboration and exchange among learners.

concepts.label: Testing effect
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use effortful recall with corrective feedback as a learning activity rather than treating quizzes only as measurement.
concepts.card: The testing effect is the finding that recalling studied material can strengthen later retention, rather than merely measure it. Closed-book questions ask learners to retrieve an answer instead of rereading it. Corrective feedback helps when recall fails, making quizzes useful as learning activities as well as assessments.

evidence.note: Checked recall-versus-rereading distinction and feedback; retained baseline Testing effect identity instead of creating a duplicate retrieval-practice card.

relations.note: The IES guide discusses retrieval and delayed re-exposure as complementary learning approaches; their mechanisms remain distinct from one another.

imported_records.description: memory effect in educational psychology

concepts.label: Spacing effect
concepts.learning_takeaway: Separate encounters with course material over time while keeping total study time comparable.
concepts.card: The spacing effect concerns better retention when study encounters are spread out rather than crowded together. The IES guide recommends returning to important material after a delay, including through reviews or quizzes. The useful interval depends on how long the knowledge must be retained, not one universal schedule.
concepts.original_description: psychological effect that people learn more by spreading studying out in time

evidence.note: Checked distributed encounters and retention-interval qualification; retained Q1095859 rather than treating instructional wording as a new identity.

relations.note: The guide explicitly proposes quizzes as one way to arrange delayed re-exposure, linking spacing with retrieval while distinguishing them.

imported_records.description: psychological effect that people learn more by spreading studying out in time

concepts.label: Interleaved practice
concepts.learning_takeaway: Mix different mathematical problem types so learners must select a strategy instead of repeating one blocked routine.
concepts.card: Interleaved practice mixes different kinds of problems rather than grouping one type into a long block. In the cited mathematics intervention, students had to choose a suitable strategy for each problem. The challenge is partly recognizing which method applies, not simply carrying out a method already signaled by repetition.

evidence.locator: Structured Abstract, Intervention and Control Condition
evidence.note: Checked the mathematics intervention's ordering manipulation and strategy-selection rationale; not claimed effective for every subject or identical to spacing.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: Mixing problem types concerns strategy selection, whereas spacing concerns timing of repeated encounters; the sources provide distinct instructional dimensions to compare.

relations.note: Mixing problem types concerns strategy selection, whereas spacing concerns timing of repeated encounters; the sources provide distinct instructional dimensions to compare.

concepts.label: Worked example
concepts.learning_takeaway: Study a demonstrated solution path before attempting comparable problems, especially while building initial expertise.
concepts.card: A worked example shows a solution path rather than asking a beginner to discover every step unaided. Studying examples alongside similar problems can focus attention on how the procedure works. The IES guide also notes that the appropriate amount of guidance changes as learners develop greater expertise.

evidence.note: Checked demonstrated solutions, alternating practice, and expertise qualification; no claim that worked examples should replace all problem solving.

relations.note: The worked-example recommendation explicitly discusses gradually fading examples as expertise increases.

concepts.label: Faded worked examples
concepts.learning_takeaway: Gradually remove later solution steps so learners supply more of the solution as expertise develops.
concepts.card: Faded worked examples gradually turn a demonstrated solution into a problem the learner completes. Early steps may remain visible while later steps are removed. As expertise develops, learners supply more of the solution themselves, creating a transition from studying a model to carrying out the procedure independently.

evidence.note: Checked direction of fading and expertise-dependent increase in responsibility; not merely shortening an explanation arbitrarily.

relations.note: The guide explicitly describes fading by retaining early steps and requiring progressively more later steps from learners.

concepts.label: Coordinating graphics and verbal explanations
concepts.learning_takeaway: Place relevant verbal explanations alongside the visual elements they explain so learners can connect representations.
concepts.card: Coordinating graphics with verbal explanations helps learners connect what an image shows with the process being described. Relevant labels can sit close to the visual elements they explain. Decorative or overly detailed pictures may distract instead, so the principle concerns meaningful integration rather than adding images indiscriminately.

evidence.note: Checked near-element labels, relevant graphics, and distracting-detail caveat; no visual/verbal learning-style categories are implied.

relations.note: The guide links visual/verbal integration with connections between representations, while the second method specifically connects concrete examples to abstract ideas.

concepts.label: Connecting concrete and abstract representations
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explicitly map familiar objects or examples onto abstract symbols so knowledge can transfer beyond surface features.
concepts.card: Connecting concrete and abstract representations means explicitly showing how familiar examples correspond to symbols or general concepts. Without that bridge, learners may manipulate a formula yet struggle to apply it elsewhere. Comparing several representations can direct attention away from surface details toward the underlying relation.

evidence.note: Checked explicit mappings and risk of inert knowledge; transfer is a goal of the method, not an automatic outcome in every setting.

relations.note: The guide's mapping between examples and abstract symbols complements, but is not identical to, coordinating words and pictures.

concepts.label: Prequestioning
concepts.learning_takeaway: Ask questions before exposure to focus study, while preserving attention to material the questions do not cover.
concepts.card: Prequestioning asks learners questions before they encounter new material. This can activate relevant knowledge and direct attention to what they need to learn. The cited guide cautions that selective reading may neglect material not covered by the questions, and its classroom evidence for this recommendation was limited.

evidence.note: Checked pre-exposure timing, attention rationale, nonquestioned-material risk, and the guide's low-evidence classification rather than asserting a universal benefit.

relations.note: Questions before exposure differ from retrieving already studied material; contrasting them prevents all uses of quizzes being treated as one testing mechanism.

concepts.label: Delayed judgments of learning
concepts.learning_takeaway: After a delay, use only a cue to judge future recall so immediate familiarity is less misleading.
concepts.card: A delayed judgment of learning asks someone to estimate future recall after time away from the material, using a cue without the answer visible. The delay reduces reliance on immediate familiarity. The cited guide treats this as promising for allocating study, while noting limited classroom evidence.

evidence.note: Checked delay, cue-only access, prospective judgment, and low classroom-evidence rating; not equated with an immediate confidence rating or actual test performance.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: Both approaches use information to guide subsequent learning, but a learner's delayed recall estimate is distinct from the broader formative use of assessment evidence.

relations.note: Both approaches use information to guide subsequent learning, but a learner's delayed recall estimate is distinct from the broader formative use of assessment evidence.

concepts.label: Self-explanation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Generate one's own causal or logical explanations during study rather than merely repeating the presented answer.
concepts.card: Self-explanation asks learners to produce their own account of why an idea or solution works. Saying the steps aloud is useful only if it connects them to causes, principles, or reasons. The IES guide encourages explanatory questions and feedback rather than treating repetition of an answer as understanding.

evidence.note: Checked deep causal/logical explanations and think-aloud guidance; simple verbatim repetition is not equated with the explanatory process.

relations.note: Explaining why steps work can complement studying a worked solution; the guide treats explanation generation and displayed examples as different instructional supports.

concepts.label: Formative assessment
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use evidence during learning to adjust teaching and study, with purpose mattering more than a test's format.
concepts.card: Formative assessment uses evidence during learning to improve what happens next. An instructor may identify a misconception and adjust teaching, while a learner redirects study. The defining feature is this feedback purpose: even information from a final exam can later be used formatively in another course.

evidence.note: Checked ongoing feedback and later formative use of summative information; low stakes is typical rather than a necessary definition.

evidence.locator: What is it?; distinction from teaching for mastery
evidence.note: Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: Mastery learning uses checks and corrective support to guide progression, providing a specific comparison with formative assessment's broader feedback purpose.

relations.note: Mastery learning uses checks and corrective support to guide progression, providing a specific comparison with formative assessment's broader feedback purpose.

concepts.label: Mastery learning
concepts.learning_takeaway: Hold learning goals steady while varying time and corrective support before progression to new units.
concepts.card: Mastery learning holds intended outcomes steady while allowing time and support to vary. Learners work through units, demonstrate sufficient understanding, and receive additional help when needed before progressing. Approaches differ in their thresholds and organization, so aiming for mastery is not itself one uniform teaching procedure.

evidence.locator: What is it?; distinction from teaching for mastery
evidence.note: Checked fixed goals, variable time/support and variation among implementations; avoided conflating mastery learning with every approach called teaching for mastery.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: Using unit-test evidence to provide corrective support before progression applies the formative feedback idea within a particular instructional model.

relations.note: Using unit-test evidence to provide corrective support before progression applies the formative feedback idea within a particular instructional model.

concepts.label: Eric Mazur
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore how a physicist's course redesign made individual commitments and peer reasoning part of lectures.
concepts.card: Eric Mazur's work on Peer Instruction helped redesign introductory physics lectures around students' reasoning. In the reported courses, learners answered conceptual questions individually, discussed their explanations, and voted again. The case makes a teaching method inspectable through its sequence of activities rather than a lecturer's reputation alone.

evidence.note: Checked coauthorship and course design; did not attribute every result solely to discussion because other course elements also changed.

relations.note: The coauthored paper directly documents Mazur's implementation of Peer Instruction and describes its question/discussion/revote sequence.

concepts.label: Peer Instruction
concepts.learning_takeaway: Sequence an individual conceptual answer, peer explanation, a second vote, and instructor feedback during class.
concepts.card: Peer Instruction inserts conceptual questions into a lecture. Students first commit to individual answers, explain their reasoning to nearby peers, then answer again before the instructor explains. The sequence gives discussion a specific job: compare reasons and reconsider an answer, rather than simply listen to another mini-lecture.

evidence.note: Checked initial answer, discussion, second poll and instructor feedback; not claimed that all answers improve or that every peer-learning format follows this protocol.

relations.note: The paper directly describes structured peer explanation as the central collaborative activity within its classroom protocol.

concepts.label: Economics
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect choices under scarce resources with the gains and coordination problems of specialization and exchange.
concepts.card: Economics studies how people and societies make choices when resources are limited. Specialization can increase what people produce, but it also makes them depend on exchange and coordination. Studying those choices includes asking how information, incentives, and institutions affect whether the potential gains are actually realized.
concepts.original_description: social science that studies the production, distribution, and consumption of goods and services

evidence.note: Checked scarcity and specialization from the introduction and information-related trade obstacles from section 16.1; no claim that monetary value measures every human goal.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The introductory scarcity-and-exchange framework leads to the specific question of how unequal information can obstruct mutually beneficial transactions.

relations.note: The introductory scarcity-and-exchange framework leads to the specific question of how unequal information can obstruct mutually beneficial transactions.

concepts.label: Information asymmetry
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish unequal knowledge between parties from uncertainty that both sides share.
concepts.card: Information asymmetry occurs when one party to a transaction knows more relevant information than another. A used-car seller may know defects the buyer cannot readily observe. This differs from shared uncertainty: both parties can lack information, but asymmetry describes an unequal distribution of what they know.

evidence.note: Checked unequal versus incomplete information and used-car example; unequal knowledge need not imply deliberate dishonesty in every transaction.

Supplementary inspected premise for the card or its comparison: The insurance chapter explicitly links privately known risk to adverse selection, providing a concrete consequence of information asymmetry.

relations.note: The insurance chapter explicitly links privately known risk to adverse selection, providing a concrete consequence of information asymmetry.

concepts.label: Adverse selection
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how privately known risk changes which people seek insurance and can push low-risk buyers out.
concepts.card: Adverse selection can arise when insurance buyers know more about their own risk than the insurer. A pooled premium may attract high-risk buyers while discouraging lower-risk ones. The changing mix can then raise average claims, making coverage harder to price even before anyone changes their behavior.

evidence.note: Checked buyer composition, pooled pricing and before-versus-after agreement distinction; not every insurance pool is claimed to unravel.

relations.note: The insurance source contrasts hidden-risk selection with behavior changes after coverage; the comparison separates two different information problems.

concepts.label: Moral hazard
concepts.learning_takeaway: Trace how protection from losses can change behavior after insurance is in place.
concepts.card: Moral hazard describes how protection from consequences can change behavior after an agreement. Insurance may reduce the incentive to prevent a loss when another party pays much of the cost. Insurers use monitoring and cost sharing to address this problem, although they cannot observe every risky action.

evidence.note: Checked incentive mechanism, limited observation and mitigation; avoided using the term as a judgment about a person's moral character.

relations.note: The insurance chapter explicitly presents deductibles and other cost-sharing arrangements as ways to reduce moral-hazard incentives.

concepts.label: Signaling in economics
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use observable credentials or actions to convey information about otherwise hidden qualities.
concepts.card: Economic signaling uses observable actions or credentials to convey information about less visible qualities. A prospective worker's qualifications may help an employer infer preparation or persistence. The signal does not remove all uncertainty; it offers evidence about something the employer cannot fully observe before hiring.

evidence.note: Checked credential-as-signal example and remaining uncertainty; not claimed that a credential perfectly measures ability or always forms a separating equilibrium.

relations.note: The source's credential and employer-investigation examples support distinguishing information supplied by the informed party from screening initiated by the less-informed party.

concepts.label: Screening in economics
concepts.learning_takeaway: Let a less-informed party investigate or set requirements to learn hidden characteristics before a transaction.
concepts.card: Screening is an effort by the less-informed side of a transaction to learn relevant hidden characteristics. A buyer may have a mechanic inspect a used car, or an employer may check references. This reverses the initiative in signaling, where the better-informed party supplies an observable indication.

evidence.note: Checked mechanic inspection, employer inquiries and direction of initiative; did not import unsupported contract-menu claims from inaccessible Nobel pages.

relations.note: The inspected examples distinguish the investigator's effort to gather information from the informed party's presentation of a signal.

concepts.label: Reputation in markets
concepts.learning_takeaway: Make future business valuable enough that sellers have a reason to preserve buyers' trust.
concepts.card: A seller's reputation can make future business depend on how current customers are treated. Passing off a poor-quality product may earn money now but lose repeat customers and recommendations later. This gives buyers a reason to consider the seller's ongoing stake, alongside the product they can inspect.

evidence.note: Checked short-term versus future-business incentives and repeat-customer mechanism; reputation is not treated as proof that a product is good.

relations.note: The textbook explicitly discusses reputation together with guarantees, warranties and service contracts as responses to buyers' quality uncertainty.

concepts.label: Warranties as quality assurance
concepts.learning_takeaway: Shift specified repair or replacement obligations to a seller so buyers need not verify every quality claim beforehand.
concepts.card: A warranty promises specified repair or replacement if a product fails within agreed conditions. It reduces the need for buyers to verify every aspect of quality before purchase by assigning some consequences to the seller. Its protection depends on the actual terms, rather than the label alone.

evidence.note: Checked repair/replacement commitment and time qualification; no assertion that warranties eliminate hidden defects or cover every possible failure.

relations.note: The textbook presents warranties as an explicit response to quality uncertainty between buyers and sellers; the response is distinct from the information gap itself.

concepts.label: Risk pooling
concepts.learning_takeaway: Combine many uncertain individual losses into a shared pool funded by premiums.
concepts.card: Risk pooling combines many people's uncertain losses so premiums can fund the claims that actually occur. An individual may face a large bill even when the group's average loss is manageable. How people are grouped and priced matters, especially when their risks differ or are privately known.

evidence.note: Checked shared premiums and average loss example; pooling is not said to remove all correlated or catastrophic risk.

relations.note: The insurance example moves from pooled losses to premiums based on expected claims and distinguishes actuarially fair pricing.

concepts.label: Actuarially fair insurance
concepts.learning_takeaway: Separate a premium equal to expected claims from one that also funds operating expenses and profit.
concepts.card: Actuarially fair insurance charges a premium equal to the expected claim payment for the relevant risk group. It is a benchmark, not necessarily the price an insurer can sustainably offer. Administration, other business costs, and profit require additional funding beyond that expected-claims amount.

evidence.note: Checked expected payment definition and excluded expense/profit loading; fairness here is a technical pricing term rather than an ethical verdict.

relations.note: The source explicitly derives insurance premiums from group losses before distinguishing expected claims from operating costs and profit.

concepts.label: Insurance deductible
concepts.learning_takeaway: Require an initial out-of-pocket loss amount before the insurance coverage begins paying.
concepts.card: An insurance deductible is an amount the policyholder pays before specified coverage starts paying. It leaves some loss with the insured party instead of transferring every cost to the insurer. In the textbook's incentive account, retaining that stake can discourage risk-taking that full coverage might otherwise encourage.

evidence.note: Checked threshold structure and qualified incentive rationale; not advice about an appropriate deductible for any person or policy.

relations.note: The moral-hazard section explicitly identifies deductibles as a cost-sharing method intended to preserve incentives to avoid losses.

concepts.label: Coinsurance
concepts.learning_takeaway: Split a covered loss by percentages so the insured party retains part of each covered cost.
concepts.card: Coinsurance divides a covered cost by percentages between an insurer and the insured party. If coverage pays eighty percent, the other share remains with the policyholder. This differs from a deductible's initial threshold and a copayment's fixed charge, although a policy may combine cost-sharing mechanisms.

evidence.note: Checked percentage example and distinction among the three mechanisms; no claim about the exact ordering of charges in a particular contract.

relations.note: The textbook directly contrasts percentage sharing with deductibles and fixed copayments within its cost-sharing discussion.

concepts.label: Bond (finance)
concepts.learning_takeaway: Treat a bond as an issuer's debt promise to pay specified interest and principal, with default still possible.
concepts.card: A financial bond is a debt security: investors lend money to an issuer under specified payment terms. The issuer promises interest and repayment of principal at maturity, but may default. This meaning concerns a financial obligation, separate from the chemical bonds that hold atoms together.

evidence.locator: What are bonds?; What are the benefits and risks?
evidence.note: Checked debt, issuer payments, maturity and default. Chemical-bond sense is separately pinned as Q44424 in the approved identity review; the names are not merged.

relations.note: Investor.gov explicitly lists interest-rate risk among the risks of bonds and explains the effect on an older bond's resale value.

concepts.label: Interest-rate risk in bonds
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why an older fixed-rate bond may need a price discount when newly issued bonds offer higher rates.
concepts.card: A bond's resale value can change when market interest rates move. If newer bonds offer higher interest, an older fixed-rate bond may need to sell at a discount to attract buyers. This price risk is distinct from an issuer failing to make its promised payments.

evidence.locator: What are the benefits and risks of bonds?, Interest rate risk
evidence.note: Checked old-versus-new coupon comparison and resale qualification; not claimed that every bond has identical sensitivity or that maturity eliminates default risk.

relations.note: Investor.gov explicitly distinguishes interest-rate risk from credit risk in its bond-risk explanation.

concepts.label: Common-value auction
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish shared underlying value from bidders' differing information about that value.
concepts.card: In a common-value auction, the object has the same underlying value to bidders, but they may estimate it differently. A jar of coins is a simple example. Winning can then reveal that one's estimate was unusually optimistic, so the information contained in winning matters for sensible bidding.

evidence.note: Checked shared value versus different estimates and winner information; real auctions can combine common and private components.

relations.note: The Yale lecture introduces the winner's curse through its common-value coin-jar auction and explains conditioning on winning.

concepts.label: Private-value auction
concepts.learning_takeaway: Model each bidder's value as personal and unaffected by learning others' valuations, an idealized limiting case.
concepts.card: A private-value auction models each bidder's valuation as personal: learning that someone else values the object highly does not change one's own value. It is an idealized case. A house, for example, may mix personal enjoyment with resale concerns that introduce a common-value component.

evidence.note: Checked independence of personal value from others' valuations and mixed housing example; private value is not equated with secret bidding.

relations.note: The lecture explicitly contrasts the two limiting valuation models and uses housing to illustrate mixtures between them.

concepts.label: Winner's curse
concepts.learning_takeaway: Condition an estimate on winning because the highest bid may reveal an unusually optimistic initial estimate.
concepts.card: The winner's curse can occur when the highest bidder also has an unusually high estimate of a shared uncertain value. Winning provides information about how optimistic that estimate was relative to others. Accounting for this selection before bidding differs from simply paying what one's initial estimate suggested.

evidence.note: Checked conditional-selection explanation; winning is not claimed to inevitably cause a loss when bidders already account for the effect.

relations.note: The lecture develops the winner's curse specifically through common-value bidding and the information revealed by winning.

concepts.label: First-price sealed-bid auction
concepts.learning_takeaway: Submit bids privately and let the highest bidder win while paying their own bid.
concepts.card: In a first-price sealed-bid auction, bidders submit offers privately, the highest bidder wins, and the winner pays their own bid. The bid therefore helps determine both the chance of winning and the payment if successful. That payment rule differs from a second-price auction.

evidence.note: Checked sealed submission, highest-bid winner and own payment; no unqualified optimal-bidding formula or revenue comparison is asserted.

relations.note: The Yale lecture directly compares highest-bid allocation with own-bid versus second-highest-bid payment rules.

concepts.label: Second-price sealed-bid auction
concepts.learning_takeaway: Award the item to the highest bidder but charge the second-highest submitted bid.
concepts.card: A second-price sealed-bid auction gives the item to the highest bidder but charges the second-highest bid. The allocation rule resembles a first-price auction, while the payment rule differs. Also called a Vickrey auction, it separates the winning offer from the amount the winner actually pays.

evidence.note: Checked highest-versus-second-highest distinction; truthful bidding is not asserted without its private-value assumptions.

relations.note: The lecture explicitly names Vickrey auctions and contrasts their payment rule with first-price sealed bidding.

concepts.label: Ascending open auction
concepts.learning_takeaway: Reveal progressively higher offers until only one bidder remains willing to pay the rising price.
concepts.card: An ascending open auction raises the price while bidders remain active or drop out. When only one bidder remains willing to continue, that bidder wins. Unlike sealed bids, the process makes others' continued participation visible, so the sequence itself can convey information during the auction.

evidence.note: Checked rising-price/dropout mechanism and observable participation; no claim that every online auction implements this exact format.

relations.note: The lecture contrasts open ascending participation with privately submitted sealed bids, explaining each format's sequence.
